subject: Chemistry
title: Why Coins Turn Green
description: A fast breakdown of Why Coins Turn Green for builders.

hook.text: Old copper coins, the Statue of Liberty, and church domes all turn green for the same chemical reason.

buildup.text: Copper reacts with oxygen in air to form a thin layer of copper oxide—a dark brown coating.

discovery.text: Over time, copper oxide reacts further with CO₂ and moisture to form copper carbonate—a green mineral called patina.

twist.text: The Statue of Liberty was originally copper-brown. It took about 20 years for the green patina to fully develop.

climax.text: Patina actually protects the copper beneath from further corrosion. The green layer is self-defense.

punchline.text: Copper plus air plus time equals green. The patina is armor, not damage.

quiz.question: What causes the green color on old copper objects?
options: Copper carbonate (patina) formed by reaction with air, CO₂, and moisture
Algae growing on the metal surface

details.summary: Copper coins and structures turn green when copper reacts with oxygen, water, and carbon dioxide over time to form copper carbonate, commonly called verdigris or patina. This green layer actually protects the underlying copper from further corrosion, which is why copper roofs can last for centuries.
details.whyItMatters: Copper patina is a natural example of a passivation layer, a concept used throughout materials science and engineering to protect metals from environmental degradation.
takeaways: Copper oxidizes to form a protective green copper carbonate layer
The patina acts as a passivation layer that prevents further corrosion
The Statue of Liberty's green color comes from a century of copper patina

faq.question: How long does it take for copper to develop a green patina?
faq.answer: The timeline depends on environmental conditions. In coastal or industrial areas with salt and sulfur in the air, patina can develop within five to seven years. In drier, cleaner environments it may take twenty years or more. The Statue of Liberty took about twenty years to turn fully green.

faq.question: Is the green patina on copper the same as rust on iron?
faq.answer: No. Iron rust is porous and flaky, allowing oxygen and moisture to reach fresh iron underneath, so corrosion continues until the metal is consumed. Copper patina forms a dense, adherent layer that seals the surface. This is why copper lasts centuries while unprotected iron rusts away.
